items.title: 10.2.2 Finding the oxidation number of an element in a compound or a radical

source_refs.note: Topic 10.2.2 with Samples 10.1 to 10.3, printed pages 215-216. The arithmetic slip in Sample 10.3 is noted.

blocks.text: The oxidation number of any atom in a compound or a radical is found from the rules above. In compounds of a metal with a non-metal the metal always has the positive oxidation number and the non-metal the negative one: in sodium sulfide, Na2S, 2(+1) + S = 0, so S = -2. In compounds of two different non-metals the sign depends on electronegativity, the most electronegative element taking the negative sign.
Each O atom is -2, so two oxygen atoms give 2 x (-2) = -4. SO2 has no charge, so the total is zero: S + 2(-2) = 0, S - 4 = 0, S = +4.
Compound ions are ions with two or more different atoms, such as the sulfate ion SO4 2- and the nitrate ion NO3-. For sulfate, [Ox. No. of S] + 4 [Ox. No. of O] = -2, so S + 4(-2) = -2 and S = +6.
(Ox. No. of K) + (Ox. No. of Mn) + 4 (Ox. No. of O) = 0, so +1 + Mn + 4(-2) = 0, Mn - 7 = 0, Mn = +7.
